en: The first is that the change is just the normal working of the software, a tweak, an update or a balance pass. But this industry language hides the normative core under engineering vocabulary, because when the platform unilaterally alters a rare cosmetic item or redesigns a character, it determines by code the material conditions of enjoyment and the way the good will be recognized and compared in the social world of the game. If the alteration lowers the functional and symbolic value that motivated the acquisition, the problem stops being user nostalgia and becomes an architectural redefinition of the content delivered, with a direct effect on auditability and attribution, which remain here as a horizon, with no conclusion of abusiveness.

This point requalifies the usual language of the industry, which tends to hide the normative core under engineering vocabulary (“tweak”, “update”, “balancing”). When a platform unilaterally alters a rare cosmetic item or redesigns a character, it is determining, by code, the material conditions of enjoyment and the way the good will be recognized and compared in the social world of the game. If the alteration lowers the functional and symbolic value that motivated the acquisition, the problem is not “user nostalgia”, but an architectural redefinition of the content delivered, with a direct impact on auditability and on the attribution of abusiveness.<1>p. 135</1>

The second inverts Ellul's argument and holds that, if technique is autonomous, nothing would be anyone's decision. This reading fails, because the inevitability Ellul speaks of is a critical description of a system effect, the tendency of the technical to naturalize and justify itself, and not a claim that history is closed to contestation. Saying that technique acquires autonomy does not mean assuming a single, inevitable or monolithic causality, but recognizing that, in certain arrangements, incentives make the implementation of systems partly self-fueling, often without public deliberation proportional to its effects. The legal problem lies between that tendency and the possibility of democratic governance, and Ellul himself ends his work with an appeal to individual and collective responsibility in the face of technique.

The Ellulian reference to “inevitability” must be taken as a critical description of a system effect, that is, of the tendency toward naturalization and self-justification of the technical, and not as a normative thesis according to which history would be closed to contestation.<1>p. 96</1>

Saying that technique acquires “autonomy” does not mean postulating a single, inevitable or monolithic causality, but recognizing that, in certain sociotechnical arrangements, institutional and economic incentives turn the innovation and implementation of systems into a partly self-fueling dynamic, frequently dissociated from public deliberation proportional to its effects. It is precisely in this space, between systemic tendency and the possibility of democratic governance, that the legal problem in question lies.<1>p. 88</1>

At the end of his work, Ellul questions the belief that technical progress is an objective synonym for human progress and makes an appeal to individual and collective responsibility in the face of technique <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 441-445)</2>.<3>p. 96</3>

The third is that everything was in the terms and the consumer was warned. The contractual text does not lose importance, but examining design has two consequences. Design must be treated as a material dimension of supply, because it is where the practical rules of access, permanence and loss are stabilized. Legal control cannot depend only on general clauses or advertising promises, since it must reach the mechanisms through which the platform produces equivalences, lowers values and applies modulations without sufficient transparency.

Consumer Law cannot confine itself to checking clauses or isolated informational duties when experience, enjoyment and loss are conditioned by technical decisions embedded in the environment.<1>p. 137</1>

The first consequence is that design must be treated as a material dimension of supply, because the practical rules of access, permanence and loss that define the enjoyment of the immaterial object are stabilized in it. The second is that, if architecture concentrates teleologies and condenses ambivalent functions, legal control cannot depend only on general clauses or advertising promises, and must reach the mechanisms by which the platform produces equivalences, lowers values and applies modulations without sufficient transparency.<1>p. 137</1>

The fourth is that the critique would be moralizing or opposed to technology. The very choice of authors rules out this objection. Postman matters not as nostalgia for print culture, but as a key to understanding that each medium sets up its own ecology of perception and knowledge. The shift carried out by Feenberg, which moves rationality from the plane of an abstract ideal to that of an operating social function, serves precisely so that the consumer law critique is not confused with a moralizing refusal of technique. What is reconstructed is a regime of power whose effectiveness is produced by systems, standards and decision routines embedded in infrastructures.
Postman's contribution matters not as nostalgia for print culture, but as a key to understanding that each medium sets up its own ecology of perception and knowledge.<1>p. 98</1>

By shifting rationality from the domain of an abstract ideal to that of an operating social function, Feenberg provides the bridge needed for the consumer law critique not to be confused with a moralizing refusal of technique. What is reconstructed is a regime of power whose effectiveness is produced by systems, standards and decision routines embedded in infrastructures <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 15-16)</2>.<3>p. 123</3>
Does the diagnosis of technique create law?

The diagnosis does not create law by itself. The reference to positive software law does not anticipate the later dogmatic construction, and the categories that depend on this background, such as semiotic vulnerability, abusive teleology, open auditability and functional value equivalence, are built only in their own chapters. Nothing said here supports the conclusion that every update is unlawful, because updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility in a competitive ecosystem, and not every improvement becomes a legal problem.

For the purposes of this section, the reference does not anticipate the later dogmatic construction; it only shows that dependence on maintenance, updating and governance over time is not an accident external to the consumer relationship, but an attributable feature of supply in digital environments.<1>p. 91</1>

The authors also come with limits of use that the jurist must respect. Ellul is brought in not for a generic critique of technological modernity, but to make intelligible the technical order in which the IOC is formed. Postman matters less for his sectoral object, television, than for the mechanism. The parallel between Vanderburg and Durkheim works by analogy, comparing the functions of belonging, validation and sanction that metrics and infrastructures take on with those Durkheim describes in the symbolic regime. Feenberg's industrial example counts for its structural function, not for being digital.
Ellul is not summoned to support a generic critique of technological modernity, but to make intelligible the technical order in which the IOC is formed.<1>p. 97</1>
The conversion of public space into show business matters less for its sectoral object than for its mechanism.<1>p. 101</1>

Technical-operational modernity compresses dense symbolic mediations without eliminating the structural need for symbolization; it shifts, however, its supports and criteria of validity to artifacts, devices and functional grammars, opening space for metrics, performances and access infrastructures to take on, in practice, functions of belonging, validation and sanction comparable, by analogy, to those Durkheim describes in the symbolic regime, converting technical governance into lived moral routine.<1>p. 108</1>

Care is also needed with the evidentiary material. The empirical dimension is illustrative and disciplined by mechanisms, with no claim to describe the ecosystem in full or to show statistical prevalence, and the Riot Games examples serve to make institutional arrangements and legally relevant points of friction intelligible. Entries from collaborative repositories, such as the game's wiki, come in only as technical-operational support and as a lead for locating primary documentation, and never to prove institutional promises, internal decision criteria or official milestones of change.

The empirical dimension of the work is mobilized for an illustrative purpose and disciplined by mechanisms, so as to make intelligible institutional arrangements and legally relevant points of friction. There is no intention to describe the ecosystem exhaustively, nor to demonstrate statistical prevalence, nor to offer a complete overview of its history or its variations.<1>p. 49</1>

As to the status of the subsidiary use of collaborative repositories (such as Fandom) for naming categories and minimal operational description of mechanics, the criterion already set in Chapter 2 is adopted, according to which this material is not used to prove institutional promises, internal decision criteria or official milestones of change, operating only as technical-operational support and as a lead for locating primary documentation when this becomes necessary.<1>p. 94</1>

Semiotic vulnerability

Semiotic vulnerability is the form the consumer's factual vulnerability takes when the platform controls the signs, metrics, visibility and records through which the consumer understands what they acquired, perceives what they lost and tries to prove the loss. In these environments formally informed consent is not enough, and the category fits Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> without creating a new vulnerability.
Why does available information not protect the platform consumer?

In platform ecosystems, experience is administered in flow, value is modulated over time and loss may arise as an ordinary effect of design, and not as an exceptional failure. The classic grammar of product and service, conceived for stability, one-off delivery and defects visible on inspection, grasps this picture poorly. Protecting continuous digital consumption requires identifying what kind of power operates when enjoyment depends on mutable private architecture, permanent curation and regimes of signs that organize perception, expectation and behavior.

The problem can no longer be satisfactorily grasped through the classic grammar of product or service, conceived under assumptions of stability, one-off delivery and defects knowable by relatively direct inspection. In platform ecosystems, experience is administered in flow, value is modulated over time and loss may arise not as an exceptional failure, but as an ordinary effect of design.<1>p. 501</1>

The legal protection of continuous digital consumption requires more than the mechanical extension of consolidated categories to new realities. It requires identifying, with dogmatic precision, what kind of power operates when the enjoyment of an immaterial object depends on mutable private architecture, permanent curation and regimes of signs that organize perception, expectation and behavior.<1>p. 501</1>

The common reading treats the asymmetry as a lack of data and the remedy as more information, or resorts to the figure of the consumer who did not read the contract. This reading does not hold, because the consumer decides and remains within a field of meaning they cannot audit, since the correspondence between the sign and the delivery depends on curations, metrics and continuous adjustments beyond their reach and, often, outside the very text of the offer. Information may exist and still not operate as practical guidance.

Under these conditions, the vulnerability that matters cannot be reduced to a lack of information or to the old model of the consumer who “did not read” or “did not understand” the contract.<1>p. 265</1>

The consumer decides and remains within a field of meaning they cannot audit, because the correspondence between the sign and the delivery depends on curations, metrics and continuous adjustments that are beyond their reach and, often, outside even the formal text of the offer.<1>p. 265</1>

This asymmetry is structural, because it stems from concentrated control of infrastructure, rules and visibility channels, semiotic, because it bears on the production of the very codes of value, reputation and equivalence of delivery, and institutional, because it is stabilized by private procedures of sanction and unilateral modulation, often opaque and hard to contest. The jurist's question therefore shifts.
The central question is no longer only whether something was disclosed, but whether it could be understood, compared and actually verified in terms compatible with consumer protection.<1>p. 501</1>

In this context, the asymmetry between supplier and consumer is not merely informational. It is structural, semiotic and institutional. It is structural because it stems from concentrated control of infrastructure, rules and visibility channels. It is semiotic because it bears on the production of the very codes of value, reputation and equivalence of delivery. It is institutional because it is stabilized by private procedures of adjudication, sanction and unilateral modulation, often opaque and with low contestability.<1>p. 263</1>
What changes for the jurist when the sign is part of the good?

Semiotics enters the reasoning for a practical reason. In immaterial consumption, capture is not sustained by a clause or a technical barrier alone, and a decisive part of value is produced in the way the offer is presented, circulates and becomes recognizable as delivery. The offer is twofold, because it combines a narrative promise, which presents rarity, belonging and prestige as if they were properties of the item, with an infrastructure that sustains that meaning only while the environment keeps it intelligible to others.

In immaterial consumption, capture is not sustained only by a clause or a technical barrier. It is sustained by a regime of presentation, visibility and production of meaning that turns choice into conduct and turns enjoyment into permanence. That is why the description of the phenomenon must incorporate the semiotic dimension, since a decisive part of value is produced and stabilized in the way the offer is presented, circulates and becomes recognizable as “delivery”.<1>p. 264</1>

The offer, here, is always twofold, because it is made up of a narrative promise and a supporting infrastructure. It is narrative because it presents meaning, rarity, belonging and prestige as if they were natural properties of the item. It is infrastructure because it exists only while the technical-media environment maintains the intelligibility of that meaning and the possibility of living it before others.<1>p. 264</1>

Umberto Eco provides the descriptive instrument for establishing the sign as a legally material component of the good. For Eco, the sign is a function, an operation that by convention correlates a plane of expression with a plane of content within a system. What this changes for the jurist is where value is located. If value emanates from the system and is defined by position, changes in visibility, categorization or reading script reconfigure the economic form of the good, even if the file and the minimal functionality remain intact.
The sign relevant to IOCs is not a label attached to neutral content, because the meaning of the good depends on conventional correlations governed by code.<1>p. 266</1>

Umberto Eco's semiotics enters as a descriptive instrument to fix the sign as a legally material component of the immaterial good, a practical condition of its social existence and of its technical-economic valuation.<1>p. 266</1>

In Eco, the sign is no longer treated as a static entity and comes to be understood as a function, that is, as an operation of signification that occurs when elements of a plane of expression are correlated, by convention, with elements of a plane of content within a system, which is why the analysis must focus less on signs as things and more on the semiotic functions that constitute them <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 2000, p. 83-84)</2>.<3>p. 266-267</3>

Since value emanates from the system and is defined by position, changes in visibility, categorization, interpretation scripts or connections with other signs reconfigure the very economic form of the good, even if the file, the model or the minimal functionality remain technically “intact”.<1>p. 276</1>

In League of Legends, a loading screen border tied to the ranked tier does not increase damage or improve the win rate, yet it works as a public reading instruction about effort and hierarchical standing. The Diamond border has value because it exists in contrast to Iron, Bronze and the others. The contract confirms this reading by denying ownership of Virtual Content and forbidding redemption for real-world money, which keeps the economic substance of these items within the circuit of signs the platform institutes.

In League of Legends, a loading screen border tied to the user's ranked tier, or a progression icon, does not increase damage, does not change range, does not improve the win rate. Even so, it works as a public reading instruction, since it anticipates, in a few pixels, a set of inferences about seniority, effort, reliability, threat, prestige, belonging and hierarchical place, all of this even before any gameplay action.<1>p. 268</1>
A “Diamond” border is valuable precisely because it exists in contrast to “Iron”, “Bronze”, “Silver”, “Gold”, “Platinum” and “Emerald”.<1>p. 269</1>

By stating that the user has no ownership of “Virtual Content”, that it cannot be redeemed for “real-world” money and that the company denies monetary value to data and content residing on its servers, the contract makes clear that the economic substance of this kind of item is realized, primarily, within the circuit of signs that the platform itself institutes and maintains <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 269-270</3>

The consequence that matters for litigation is that the promise cannot be audited through individual reading or by inspecting the item in isolation, because the meaning that sustains value and enjoyment is stabilized by the ecosystem's rules and records. Vulnerability, on this plane, is a structural loss of the capacity to verify, not a lapse of attention.

Under the IOC paradigm, this means that the promise is not auditable by individual reading alone, because the meaning that sustains value and enjoyment is stabilized by the ecosystem's rules and records, while the platform controls which correlations will be activated and which reading paths will be made available. Semiotic vulnerability describes, on this plane, a structural loss of the capacity to verify, and not a defect of the consumer's attention.<1>p. 281</1>
How does the signal come to take the place of delivery?

Semiotic vulnerability is the consumer's structural exposure to the platform's unilateral control of the conditions that make the promise count as delivery, when the good is a position of enjoyment. Its core is the loss of the capacity to verify and demonstrate the link between promise and enjoyment. Everyday confirmation of delivery tends to shift from that link to a link between promise and signal, so that markers of rarity, prestige and event participation may remain intact while the relevant enjoyment has already been degraded.

Semiotic vulnerability designates the consumer's structural exposure to the platform's unilateral control of the conditions that make the promise count as delivery when the good is a position of enjoyment and not an autonomous thing. It appears when intelligibility, visibility, equivalence and temporal cadence stop being background and come to make up the very mode of existence of the object, so that value depends on reading codes, public hierarchies, markers of recognition and rhythms that the environment continuously administers. That is why the core lies not in ignorance of a clause nor in an information deficit, but in the loss of the capacity to verify and demonstrate the link between promise and enjoyment in a governed ecosystem, in which what counts as “delivery” may be shifted without clear notice and without a visible rupture of the object.<1>p. 321</1>

When the good is positional, everyday confirmation of delivery tends to shift from the promise-enjoyment link to a promise-signal link, because what the ecosystem makes visible and circulable as recognition comes to work as a practical criterion of performance. Markers of rarity, belonging, prestige, updating, event participation and other labels stabilize the position as a legible and comparable difference. These signals may remain intact even when the relevant enjoyment has been degraded or reconfigured, keeping the public appearance of continuity and making the loss harder to convert into rupture.<1>p. 321</1>

The mechanism breaks down into layers. In the layer of meaning, the platform controls reading codes, categories and classifications, and the rare may become common without any overt change to the item. In the layer of visibility, it controls what appears, what is highlighted and what becomes comparable as prestige. In the layer of equivalence, it keeps the label and the frame of rarity while functions, restrictions and performance conditions change underneath. In the temporal layer, cadences, windows and cycles make value depend on continuous presence. The list of asymmetries replaces equivalence with an evidentiary asymmetry, tied to control of records, metrics and versions, and reading the two lists together ensures that neither is lost.

There is an asymmetry of meaning, tied to control of the reading codes, categories and classifications that define what counts as a relevant difference. There is an asymmetry of visibility, tied to control of the field of what appears, what is highlighted and what becomes comparable as prestige. There is a temporal asymmetry, tied to control of the cadences, windows and cycles that make value depend on continuous presence. And there is an evidentiary asymmetry, tied to control of the records, metrics, versions and internal criteria that determine what can be demonstrated later. These layers couple as a mechanism and produce a structural loss of verifiability: the central problem is not only knowing, but being able to prove.<1>p. 322</1>

The layer of meaning operates when the platform governs the intelligibility of the good without needing to alter the item overtly at the technical level, because reclassifying, recategorizing, renaming attributes and reordering repertoires alters what the object “is” for the ecosystem. An IOC may remain accessible and, even so, lose the status that made it economically operative. The rare becomes common, the distinctive becomes ordinary, the “event” item becomes noise, the sign of belonging becomes indifferent, and the difference in status that justified the acquisition is lost over an undisclosed period and without any notice.<1>p. 322</1>

The platform preserves the item's label, class, frame of rarity, form of display and comparative place, ensuring that it keeps “reading” as equivalent in the internal hierarchies, while functions, restrictions, modes of access, performance conditions and practical effects may be altered, degraded or emptied.<1>p. 323-324</1>

The layer of meaning is illustrated by the Soul Fighter Samira skin, released in 2023 under the Ultimate tier, when the company stated that the definition of Ultimate had changed over the years and admitted that the project had started as Legendary. Taste is not at issue, nor is community criticism taken as a measure of truth. What matters is that, when the category becomes a redefinable label, the platform alters by classification what counts as delivery, without needing to admit nonperformance, and proof of the link becomes contentious and costly.
An empirical case that makes this semantic instability explicit is the controversy around the Soul Fighter Samira skin, released under the Ultimate tier in 2023<1>p. 322</1>

In /dev: State of Skins 2023, when announcing Samira's Ultimate, Riot began to state that the definition of Ultimate “has changed over the years” and that the goal becomes something like best-in-class and “truly special” for the champion, also admitting that the project had started as Legendary and was only later raised to Ultimate.<1>p. 322</1>

The relevant legal point is not to discuss “taste” nor to turn community criticism into a measure of truth, but to observe how the ecosystem itself comes to depend on a unilateral redefinition of what the tier's sign promises.<1>p. 322</1>

When the platform treats the Ultimate category as a label whose definition may be rewritten over time by more open criteria, it alters, through language and classification, what counts as delivery, without needing to admit any nonperformance of what was offered.<1>p. 322-323</1>

The practical effect is to shift verification outside the point of purchase and outside the supplier's self-description, producing a regime in which proof of the promise-enjoyment link becomes contentious, socially disputed and informationally costly, precisely because what was sold as a category comes to operate as an elastic sign administered by the supplier itself.<1>p. 323</1>

Hence the change in the object of proof. The binary of working or not working no longer decides adequacy, because technical access can be kept while what made the position economically operative is lost, and what must be reconstructed are the classifications, metrics, visibility criteria, cadences, rules and equivalences in force when the promise was made. A privileged way to visualize this loss is the nerf, the deliberate weakening of attributes through an update, which the chapter on equivalence examines.
It is not enough to show that “the item exists” or that “access remains”.<1>p. 326</1>

Under these premises, the notion of adequacy cannot be decided by the binary “works/does not work”, because it is perfectly possible to keep technical access and, even so, lose what made the position economically operative.<1>p. 325</1>

The evidence required is no longer a mere inspection of the good's current state but a reconstruction of the nexus: which classifications, metrics, visibility criteria, cadences, rules and equivalences were in force when the promise was made and how they were later altered.<1>p. 326</1>

A prime way to visualize this loss of verifiability is the nerf, understood as a technically deliberate weakening of attributes, abilities or items, through a patch, to make something less powerful in the practical functioning of the game <1>League of Legends Wiki</1><2>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]m)</2>.<3>p. 328</3>
Why does the player's staying not prove free choice?

Psychopolitics comes in through what it changes in the vocabulary of choice. Byung-Chul Han holds that the positivity of power can be more efficient than the negativity of duty, and that a smart power does not discipline by prohibition, but summons the psyche to participate, exploiting freedom more than denying it. With this lens, subjection is described without individual psychological analysis and the conflict shifts from the vocabulary of choice to the conditions of governance that produce what presents itself as choice.

The shift from the disciplinary model to a regime of performance makes it possible to describe contemporary subjection without resorting to individual psychological analysis, since the axis of conformity no longer depends on external prohibitions and comes to operate through productive positivity and the internalization of demands.<1>p. 352</1>

Byung-Chul Han holds that the positivity of power can be more efficient than the negativity of duty, so that the achievement-subject tends to be faster and more productive than the subject of obedience, although this mutation does not erase discipline, since the achievement-subject remains disciplined and carries the disciplinary stage within <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2015, [p. 15])</2>.<3>p. 352</3>

Han holds that a smart power does not discipline the psyche by coercion or prohibition, but approaches it and summons it to participate and share, exploiting freedom more than denying it, precisely because it manages to operate without presenting itself as power <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 18])</2>.<3>p. 353</3>

The result matters legally because it shifts the conflict from the vocabulary of choice to the plane of the conditions of governance that produce, calibrate and make economically relevant what presents itself as choice.<1>p. 361</1>

The lens applies to the ranked regime of League of Legends. Official support states that MMR, the calculated value that measures the player, is secret, and that rank exists to translate it into an accessible form, so that the player tries to conform to an opaque criterion whose result alone they can see. That is why the ranked climb tends to turn leisure into a regime of rational self-exploitation, the figure Han describes as the individual who becomes a self-exploiting worker in their own enterprise and holds the positions of command and submission at once.

In explaining the system, official support states that MMR is secret and that rank exists as a mechanism to translate this MMR into an accessible and progressive form for the player <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026h)</2>.<3>p. 354</3>

The player's freedom is organized as a voluntary effort to conform to the criterion that measures them, even when the criterion is opaque, because what becomes visible and socially legible is the positional result, and not the workings of the calculation. That is why the ranked climb tends to turn leisure into a regime of rational self-exploitation.<1>p. 354</1>

Han describes how, in the present, each individual tends to become a self-exploiting worker in their own enterprise, combining in the same figure the positions of command and submission, and how even class struggle can be lived as an inner struggle against oneself, under conditions defined by the solitude of the isolated and self-combative entrepreneur, who practices self-exploitation voluntarily <1>Han</1><2>(Han, 2017, [p. 11])</2>.<3>p. 360-361</3>

In the Honor system, sanctions lower the level, lock progress and make the account ineligible for rewards, and the Terms of Service extend the User Rules to conduct outside the game, to streams and to social networks, with penalties that may apply in the company's other games. Discipline, in this arrangement, sets in as the subject's own everyday prudence, as they adjust their conduct so as not to lose eligibility.

In a specific document on Honor restrictions, Riot explains that sanctions such as suspension and chat restriction lower the Honor level, lock progress and make the account ineligible for rewards tied to this regime <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2017b)</2>.<3>p. 356</3>
Discipline, here, need not appear as an explicit threat, because it sets in as the subject's own everyday prudence.<1>p. 355</1>

Freedom thus operates as an operator of conformity because the subject anticipates the gaze of the ecosystem and adjusts their conduct so as not to lose eligibility. This logic spills beyond the game itself and takes on the contours of identity governance, since the Terms of Service establish that the User Rules govern behavior during the game and also certain conduct outside it, providing for disciplinary measures that may extend to temporary suspension, account termination and even hardware bans <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2><3>p. 356</3>

In addition, the contract makes explicit that the User Rules may apply to streams, recorded videos and social media posts, and allows for penalties applicable to multiple Riot services, including penalties escalated across games <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 356</3>

From this picture comes identity captivity, an expression that designates neither physical imprisonment nor inability to act, and names the practical dependence by which the continuity of enjoyment and the stability of symbolic identity come to be mediated by the ecosystem. The ranked ladder is not a detachable asset, because access comes under a revocable license and closing the account entails losing access to the environment and the associated data. The exit barrier can be described as a form of social death, in a functional sense and not as moral dramatization.

The user becomes a practical agent of their own subjection within an environment in which a third party - not bound by any effective standards of transparency - administers metrics, visibility and permanence as “legitimate” conditions of value.<1>p. 361</1>

The institutionally relevant effect of this picture can be described as identity captivity. The expression neither designates physical imprisonment nor assumes an inability to act, but names a practical dependence, by which the continuity of enjoyment and the stability of symbolic identity come to be mediated by the administered ecosystem.<1>p. 358</1>

The conditions of access and permanence are provided under a revocable and conditioned license, and account termination entails loss of access to the environment and to associated data <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2><3>p. 354-355</3>

Thus, the ranked ladder does not operate as a detachable asset. It operates as a grammar of recognition that exists only while the account and the service remain active, which makes leaving, slowing down or falling out of line more costly than they would seem under an ontology of static “product”.<1>p. 355</1>

The exit barrier can be described as a form of social death within the ecosystem. The expression does not operate as moral dramatization, but as a functional description of the effect produced when the platform concentrates the records that sustain belonging and relevance, that is, history, repertoire, ranked position, signs of prestige, community ties and traces of participation.<1>p. 359</1>

The legal consequence is that subjection is neither a moral trait nor an individual pathology, but a predictable effect of the environment, which prevents treating the problem as an asymmetry correctable by formal notice or as a competitive dynamic resolved by a market alternative. Dependence becomes exploitable in relation to parameters the consumer does not control and, as a rule, cannot verify, and it requires reinforced duties of qualified transparency, contestability, auditability and restoration. Han's formulations are deliberately charged and count for their descriptive usefulness.

The subjection described, therefore, is neither a moral trait nor an individual pathology, but a predictable effect of an environment in which performance, exposure and measurability work as a grammar of permanence.<1>p. 361</1>

This shift prevents the problem from being treated as a simple informational asymmetry correctable by formal notice, or as a neutral competitive dynamic resolved by a market alternative. The platform concentrates the administration of the variables that define what will be recognized, rewarded, downgraded and excluded, and this concentration makes the consumer's dependence on parameters they do not control, and as a rule cannot verify, exploitable.<1>p. 361-362</1>

Permanence comes to depend on continuous alignment with mutable operational standards, and leaving is no longer simple substitution of a service, because it involves a discontinuity of prestige, comparability and belonging. This dependence on administered recognition is legally relevant because it makes integrity and identity governed variables of enjoyment and requires, on the dogmatic plane, reinforced duties of qualified transparency, contestability, auditability and restoration proportional to the type of power exercised by the Lex Plataformae.<1>p. 358-359</1>

Han's formulations, though deliberately charged, help fix the point in a technically useful way, since they describe a dynamic in which the positivity of performance converts inner life into fuel for the demand to produce more, and in which the very idea of adjustment shifts from care to exhaustion.<1>p. 363</1>
How does the diagnosis become a controllable requirement?

If the platform governs meaning, access, reputation and sanction at the same time, the starting point of control is the ecosystem's regime of intelligibility, and not the information communicated to the consumer. Through access, formal autonomy is converted into administered autonomy, since it is enough to make deviant conduct costly or impracticable. Through enforcement, which is the sanction applied by the platform itself, staying inside, but less findable and less recognized, may amount to a relevant loss of the object.
Reputation, therefore, is not a side effect of consumption, but a governed component of the object enjoyed.<1>p. 387</1>

If the platform simultaneously governs meaning, access, reputation and sanction, the starting point is not “information” understood as content communicated to the consumer, but the regime of intelligibility of the ecosystem itself.<1>p. 386</1>

The consequence is that the consumer's formal autonomy is converted into administered autonomy. Deviant conduct need not be prohibited; it is enough that it be made costly, slow, invisible or technically impracticable.<1>p. 387</1>

A decisive part of enforcement occurs through visibility and eligibility: staying “inside”, but less findable, less rankable, less recommended and less recognized may amount to a relevant loss of the object in its functional and symbolic value.<1>p. 388</1>

Control, therefore, is not reduced to a checklist of abusive clauses, because the injury may occur without textual alteration, and it falls on the practical rationality of the regime, that is, which criteria exist, how they are applied, how they can be verified and which avenues of contestation are usable. Hence qualified transparency, as intelligibility of the criteria and not as more information, effective contestability, with deadlines, stages and real review, and verifiable reasoning, which turns decisions into examinable objects.
Given this design, legal control cannot be reduced to a checklist of abusive clauses, because the injury may occur without textual alteration and without evident contractual breach.<1>p. 388</1>

The focus of control must fall on the practical rationality of the regime: which criteria exist, how they are applied, how they can be verified and which avenues of contestation are effectively usable.<1>p. 388</1>

Qualified transparency does not mean “more information” in the abstract, but intelligibility of the criteria that structure enjoyment: classification standards, recommendation parameters, minimal reasons for downgrades and restrictions, explicit statement of the type of conduct or signal that triggered the measure, and communication capable of allowing an informed response. Effective contestability requires that the challenge not be a mere ritual, but an avenue with deadlines, stages, access to minimal elements of the grounds and a real possibility of review. Verifiable reasoning is not justificatory rhetoric; it is the minimal form of turning decisions into examinable objects, making it possible to control coherence, proportionality and non-discrimination.<1>p. 388</1>

The list is completed by open auditability, as external verifiability of the way the decision was produced, and functional value equivalence, as a yardstick for the point at which the appearance of supply is preserved and real utility is degraded, both with their own chapters. The passage is not rhetoric of protective expansion, but a reconstruction of the point where control applies.
Open auditability enters as a requirement of external verifiability and of control over “how” the decision was produced.<1>p. 388</1>
Functional value equivalence operates as a yardstick to capture the point at which the platform preserves the formal appearance of supply, but degrades its real utility.<1>p. 389</1>

Thus, the transition from semiotic vulnerability to operational criteria is not rhetoric of protective expansion. It is a reconstruction of the point where control applies: from the textual promise to the effective regime of value production, in which meaning, access, reputation and sanction are integrated as a mechanism of private governance.<1>p. 389</1>
Why does the problem move from knowing more to being able to react?

In the legal regime, the diagnosis translates into an operative concept. The relevant vulnerability does not stem from one-off informational asymmetries, but from a structural asymmetry of intelligibility and agency, so that the problem moves from knowing more to being able to find one's bearings and react. The consumer is subjected to internal criteria that qualify conduct, rank appearances and shape the conditions of enjoyment, without equivalent means to understand the operating logic, contest the parameters or influence the distribution of consequences. The adjective semiotic is not anchored in an individual deficit of attention or reading, but in the structure of the system of signs.

The relevant vulnerability does not stem, therefore, from one-off informational asymmetries, but from a structural asymmetry of intelligibility and agency in relation to the arrangement that governs enjoyment. When the environment controls the parameters of appearance, recognition and commensuration that structure value and belonging, and keeps opaque the criteria for distributing consequences, the possibility of planning conduct, anticipating effects and contesting decisions is structurally weakened. The problem then shifts from "knowing more" to "being able to find one's bearings and react".<1>p. 396</1>

It is vulnerability because the consumer finds themselves subjected to internal criteria that qualify conduct, rank appearances and shape objective conditions of enjoyment derived from the link between the promise of the object, as presented in the offer, and its effective delivery, as executed by the architecture of the service, without having equivalent means to fully understand the operating logic, contest its parameters or influence the distribution of consequences.<1>p. 396</1>

The qualification as semiotic is not anchored in individual deficits of attention, reading or rationality, nor is it confused with a psychological description of use. It refers to the structure of the system of signs that organizes the experience and that conditions what appears as delivery, as success, as failure and as loss within the ecosystem.<1>p. 398</1>

Inequality of intelligibility did not begin with the digital world. Luis Alberto Warat treats the semiology of power as the analysis of signification as an instrument of social control, and Maurizio Gnerre states that language is the most powerful barbed wire for blocking access to power. What is new with the platform is where the mechanism strikes, because it no longer operates only as a discursive barrier and comes to bear on the very delivery of the object.
The inequality of intelligibility that structures enjoyment and its relevant losses did not originate with the digital.<1>p. 399</1>

Warat makes this core explicit when treating the semiology of power as an analysis of how signification can work as an instrument of social control, a normalizing and disciplinary strategy and a consensus-producing formula, capable of fabricating effects of verisimilitude about the material conditions of social life <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</2>.<3>p. 399</3>

Gnerre describes language as a mechanism for blocking access to power, stating that “language constitutes the most powerful barbed wire for blocking access to power” <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 22)</2>, and defines the social function of closed codes by noting that “special languages” “exclude from communication the people of the linguistic community outside the group that uses the special language” <3>Gnerre</3><4>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 23)</4>.<5>p. 400</5>

In platform-governed regimes of enjoyment, however, this mechanism no longer operates only as a discursive barrier or a filter of access to formal arenas and comes to bear on the very delivery of the object, since enjoyment is realized through technical mediations that administer visibility, recognition and attribution of value.<1>p. 402</1>

Jean Baudrillard explains why relevant losses may occur without suppression of access, since sign-value is part of the good. The category has two faces. The structural face stems from the very arrangement that governs enjoyment, and the strategic face arises when the administration of that grammar becomes an instrument of exploitation, through selective opacities, asymmetric frictions and gradual adjustments that erode the enjoyment bundle without perceptible rupture.

When sign-value is part of the good, alterations that persistently lower the consumer's position, erase their visibility, degrade their reputation or restrict their circulation may produce a loss equivalent to the loss of the object itself, even if the “content” remains technically available.<1>p. 403</1>
Jean Baudrillard's interpretive key makes it possible to understand why relevant losses may occur without total suppression of access or formal interruption of performance.<1>p. 403</1>

The structural face stems from the very technical-organizational arrangement that governs enjoyment, since the environment produces dependence on meaning and recognition by establishing the codes, metrics and regimes of visibility through which the experience becomes intelligible and socially valued.<1>p. 403</1>

The strategic face emerges when the administration of this symbolic grammar becomes an instrument of exploitation. In this case, the same set of mediations that organizes enjoyment may be used to induce conduct, distribute costs and normalize losses through selective opacities, asymmetric frictions, reorderings of visibility and gradual adjustments that erode the enjoyment bundle without producing, at once, a perceptible total rupture.<1>p. 403</1>

Choice architecture intensifies vulnerability. Claudia Lima Marques notes that vulnerability and the new harms also come from the design and the conduct of the intermediary third party, the gatekeeper, and, with Laura Schertel Mendes and Laís Bergstein, that under the Brazilian legal framework it is possible to sanction several cases of deceptive design tied to dark interface patterns. With Vanderburg, it becomes clear that relevant degradations may be internalized as a normal cost of the service, but recognizing design as power does not convert every design decision into unlawfulness.

In continuous and platformized digital contracts, control over choice paths, frictions, contracting rhythms and conditions of permanence shifts the asymmetry to the plane of performance, in which the consumer's decision is shaped by technical mediations and by intermediaries that do not act as simple neutral channels. In this direction, Claudia Lima Marques notes that “now vulnerability and the new harms also come from the design and the conduct of the intermediary third party”, adding that this digital intermediary is the “access guardian (gatekeeper)”, increasingly dominant in the contractual “time” and “mode” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2024, [p. 3])</2>.<3>p. 404-405</3>

In this sense, the authors note that “several of these provisions are related to dark patterns, which allows us to conclude that under the Brazilian legal framework it is possible to sanction several cases of deceptive design” <1>Bergstein</1><2>(Marques; Mendes; Bergstein, 2023, [p. 4])</2>.<3>p. 405</3>

Semiotic vulnerability intensifies because technical mediation does not operate only as a neutral channel of access, but as a form of routinization of expectations and dependencies. From Vanderburg's theoretical perspective, this process can be described as the everyday sedimentation of forms of mediation that naturalize patterns of conduct and evaluation, converting certain frictions, downgrades and restrictions into expected components of the experience. The consequence is that relevant degradations may be internalized as a "normal cost" of the service, which weakens the capacity to identify the harm and shifts contestation to a terrain in which the decisive criteria remain opaque or unavailable.<1>p. 406</1>

Recognizing this dimension does not imply converting every design decision into unlawfulness, but it authorizes the analysis of design as a form of infrastructural power capable of guiding conduct and normalizing harms through technical and organizational standards.<1>p. 406</1>
What can the word buy in the game store demonstrate?

The mechanism can be observed in a single word. In the League of Legends store, the command offered to the consumer displays the word buy, which in everyday usage and in the Civil Code means acquiring something that becomes yours, with an expectation of minimal stability and permanence. Article 481 of the Civil Code<1><2>2</2></1> defines purchase and sale by the obligation to transfer ownership of a certain thing for a price. The grammar extends into the inventory, organized as a collection, a word that carries the idea of ordering a holding, preserving its history and completing series.

In the empirical laboratory under study, this mechanism can be observed without any theoretical sophistication, just by paying attention to the use of a single word. On entering the League of Legends store, the command offered to the consumer user displays the word “buy”.<1>p. 400</1>

Both everyday usage and even the Brazilian Civil Code itself use the verb “buy” to mean acquiring something that becomes “yours”, with the expectation of minimal stability, permanence and some form of control over what was acquired.<1>p. 400-401</1>

“Art. 481. By the contract of purchase and sale, one of the contracting parties undertakes to transfer ownership of a certain thing, and the other, to pay it a certain price in money.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]a)</2>.<3>p. 400</3>

The Terms of Service describe the same items as Virtual Content under an access license tied to the account, so that the interface presents a purchase and the contract requalifies the relationship as conditioned access. The point is not that the consumer did not read, but that the ecosystem organizes the decision through a sign that frames the relationship as a typical contract while reserving another regime. That is why an account block, an item removal or the architectural devaluation of the holding strike the intelligibility of the collection as a bundle of continued enjoyment.

When the platform presents digital content as part of a collection, it mobilizes this cultural expectation of permanence and converts isolated items into a patrimonial biography, even though, on the contractual plane, the same content is described as an access license tied to the account. That is why a possible account block, item removal, substantial alteration of functionality or architectural devaluation of the holding does not strike only a detachable digital unit. It strikes the intelligibility of the collection itself as a bundle of continued enjoyment, whose value depends on internal recognition, minimal stability and preservation of the relationship between the consumer, their items and the ecosystem that gives them meaning.<1>p. 401</1>

The result is an objective inequality of decoding and agency, because the consumer decides under the grammar of buying and enjoys under that of the revocable license. The word, by itself and in isolation, is not unlawful. Unlawfulness appears when a core that respects the minimal stability of the good is missing, because then the parallel becomes false and leads to the breach of the legitimate expectation of enjoyment, and what is required is responsibility for the auditability of alterations and preservation of equivalent functionality when the alteration is legitimate. What the lawyer demonstrates is a simple and verifiable friction between the interface's sign and the contract's regime, and not the client's inattention.

The result is an objective inequality of decoding and agency, because the consumer decides under the grammar of “buying”, but enjoyment is realized under the grammar of the “revocable license” tied to the account. This does not serve as grounds to state that the use of the word “buy” is, by itself and in isolation, unlawful. The point is that, without a core that respects the minimal stability of the good, even the superficial parallel becomes false and, therefore, leads to the breach of the legitimate expectation of enjoyment, only thus configuring unlawfulness.<1>p. 401-402</1>

Wild Rift, the mobile version of the game, adds the fragmentation of price. The paid currency does not tell the whole story, because consumption branches into parallel currencies tied to rewards, performance and events, each with its own circuit. An official announcement recorded an average 15% price increase for Brazil, and the contract allows changes to the purchasing power of the game currency. This difficulty is not a neutral side effect. It works as a puzzle that shifts to the consumer the burden of deciphering an economy that is costly to read.

The game's paid currency plays this role of gateway, but it does not complete the picture, because consumption branches into parallel currencies tied to rewards, performance and events, and each creates a small circuit of its own within the same service <1>Riot Games +1</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022l; Riot Games, 2025l; Riot Games, 2021d)</2>.<3>p. 397</3>

In this sense, by way of illustration, an official Wild Rift news item records price adjustments by region and mentions, for Brazil, “+15% average price increase” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2021e)</2>.<3>p. 398</3>

It is important not to forget, in this context, that Riot's contractual framework allows for changes to the “purchasing power of the Game Currency”, including by increasing the number of coins needed to acquire virtual products, and expressly denies any value “in money or otherwise” to virtual content associated with the account <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 398</3>

The experience is designed to operate in fragments of time, and value itself is fragmented along with it, as if the platform told the consumer that understanding “how much it costs” is a private effort, which must be produced within the game, “however possible” and “with whatever attention is left”. This difficulty is not a neutral side effect of the variety of systems, but operates as a deliberate puzzle, transferring to the consumer the burden of deciphering an economy that the environment designed to be costly to read.<1>p. 397</1>
Why is semiotic vulnerability not a new vulnerability?

Semiotic vulnerability is a contemporary form of the consumer's factual vulnerability, which Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> recognizes, and not a parallel or extravagant category. Claudia Lima Marques describes the consumer as the weaker party, who cannot negotiate the content of the contract, and vulnerability as the pillar of special protection. The category does not create vulnerability, because it specifies, in the context of platforms, one of the forms in which the imbalance of forces manifests itself today.

The IOC is not a new microsystem, but a new interpretive key, a way of reading the CDC itself and the Constitution, leading them to the centrality of flows of code, images, sounds and narratives in the configuration of digital consumer relations. From this perspective, the argument is that the consumer's factual vulnerability, expressly recognized in art. 4, I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, takes on a form of its own in digital environments, tied to mediation by signs, interfaces and private criteria of visibility and enjoyment.<3>p. 34</3>

The consumer's vulnerability remains the pillar of the CDC's special protection, and it is precisely for this reason that semiotic vulnerability must be understood as a contemporary specification of this structural datum, and not as a parallel or extravagant category <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 324; p. 307)</2>.<3>p. 580</3>

It is not a matter of creating a parallel category, detached from the grammar of the system, but of specifying, in the context of platforms, one of the forms in which the imbalance of forces between supplier and consumer manifests itself today. Marques states this quite directly when affirming that, in consumer contracts, "the problem is the flagrant imbalance of forces of the contracting parties. One of the parties is vulnerable (art. 4. I), it is the weaker pole of the contractual relationship, since it cannot discuss the content of the contract", being left, as a rule, only to accept or reject the predisposed package <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 324)</2>.<3>p. 580</3>

Vulnerability is articulated with good faith, the duty to inform, transparency and the protection of trust. Marques links the consumer's rational autonomy to positive duties to inform, cooperate and act loyally, and, following Ricardo Morishita Wada, information must be correct, clear, precise and conspicuous, without useless prolixity or strategic scarcity. Hence informational inadequacy is not limited to omission, since it may come through excess, dispersion or excessively technical language. Bruno Miragem adds that abusiveness may arise from the asymmetric exploitation of the relevant meanings of the relationship, and the category thus remains within the trunk of consumer law, naming more precisely a form of exploitation that its institutes already sensed.
The problem is communicational architecture that appears to inform while organizing noise.<1>p. 581</1>

The consumer's autonomy depends on positive duties to inform, cooperate, act loyally and with care, because without this minimal threshold of conduct the decision to contract is not rational in any legally relevant sense <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812; p. 1480)</2>.<3>p. 580-581</3>

It is not enough to ensure formal access to information. It must be correct, clear, precise and conspicuous, without useless prolixity or strategic scarcity, and the supplier may not erect barriers that interfere negatively with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms and conditions of the contract <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207; p. 142)</2>.<3>p. 581</3>

Abusiveness may also arise from the asymmetric exploitation of the relevant meanings of the consumer relationship, especially when lengthy, obscure or surprising clauses compromise the quality of information and the adhering party's consent <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 328-329; p. 388)</2><3>p. 582</3>

Semiotic vulnerability thus remains in the trunk of consumer law. It merely names more precisely a current form of exploitation of vulnerability already intuited by the institutes of the system.<1>p. 582</1>

The governed environment, in this reading, does not compete with the immaterial product, because it is a condition of its legal existence, and relevant alterations of the architecture may correspond to alterations of the object itself. The category reorganizes classic problems of the CDC. Delivery is no longer a pure one-off act, inadequacy is not limited to the manifest defect, identifying the defect must take into account the moment when the degradation becomes perceptible and verifiable, and the correspondence between offer and enjoyment is not measured only by the letter of the contract. Semiotic vulnerability is, therefore, a category for attributing the structural asymmetry.
In the IOC regime, the governed environment is a condition of the legal existence of the very product consumed.<1>p. 582</1>
Relevant alterations in the architecture of enjoyment may correspond, in dogmatic terms, to alterations of the very object of consumption.<1>p. 582</1>

If enjoyment depends on continuous maintenance and modulation, delivery cannot be thought of as a pure one-off act. If utility is reconfigurable, inadequacy is not limited to the manifest defect of a static thing. If there is no clear final milestone of performance, identifying the defect must engage with the real moment when the degradation becomes perceptible and verifiable. If the promise circulates through signs, advertising, narratives and interfaces, the correspondence between offer and enjoyment cannot be measured only by the literal wording of a contractual text. Semiotic vulnerability then works as a category for attributing the structural asymmetry that justifies reconstructing the duty to inform, trust, adequacy and abusiveness in an opaque and mutable environment.<1>p. 583</1>

The problem extends to proof, because the necessary evidence lies with whoever administers the logs, parameter settings and histories. Miragem observes that the technological specialization and dominant position of the supplier make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only instrument capable of making protection viable, and semiotic vulnerability is therefore also evidentiary vulnerability. The procedure is left to the chapter on proof.
The necessary evidence is not in their possession. It lies with whoever administers the environment, the logs, the parameter settings and the relevant histories.<1>p. 583</1>

The technological specialization of the service and the dominant position of the supplier make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only instrument capable of effectively making consumer protection viable <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 854; p. 283)</2><3>p. 583</3>
Why is the term digital vulnerability not enough?

The expression digital vulnerability has descriptive usefulness, but little dogmatic yield, because it names the environment in which the injury occurs and does not isolate the mechanism of the asymmetry. The digital works as a marker of setting, and not as an operator of attribution. Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. describes dogmatics as a cut in reality that isolates the problems relevant to the decision, and Miguel Reale holds that there is no raw legal fact. A concept must say what must be proven, which duty was strained and which consequence is appropriate.

The expression “digital vulnerability” will not be adopted here because, although it has descriptive usefulness, it delivers little dogmatic yield. It names the environment in which the injury occurs, but does not isolate the legally relevant mechanism of the asymmetry. The “digital” works, in this vocabulary, as a marker of setting, and not as an operator of attribution.<1>p. 584</1>

As Ferraz Jr. observes, "unlike zetetic theories, dogmatic ones, concerned with the decidability of conflicts, do not take care to be logically rigorous in the use of their concepts and definitions, since for them what matters is not the relation with the phenomena of reality (describing the phenomena), but rather making a cut in reality, isolating the problems that are relevant to decision-making and diverting attention from the others" <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 81])</2>.<3>p. 585</3>

There is no raw legal fact. There is fact legally filtered by a normative form capable of converting it into a criterion of practical discipline <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 168; p. 96)</2>.<3>p. 586</3>

A concept does not serve only to describe a socially worrying situation. It must offer a normative form stable enough that one can say what must be proven, which duty was strained or violated and which consequence is adequate to the case.<1>p. 586</1>

The label aggregates technical fragility, informational deficit, behavioral manipulation, algorithmic opacity, technological exclusion and economic asymmetry, and, by condensing so many layers, it stops indicating which one matters in each case, so that proof is dispersed and the remedy oscillates between abstraction and casuistry. Terms such as electronic, virtual or technological vulnerability reveal the perception of a new problem, but they help locate where it happens and say less about how it is produced.

“Digital vulnerability” may designate, depending on context, technical-operational fragility, informational deficit, behavioral manipulation, dependence on infrastructure, algorithmic opacity, technological exclusion or platform-mediated economic asymmetry.<1>p. 585-586</1>

The problem is that, by condensing many different layers of risk, the expression stops indicating which of them matters legally in each case. Instead of cutting the problem, it accumulates it. And, when the category accumulates too much, proof is dispersed and the remedy oscillates between excessive abstraction and casuistry.<1>p. 586</1>

The recent proliferation of expressions such as “electronic”, “virtual”, “digital” or “technological” vulnerability already reveals the perception that there is a new problem, but also the difficulty of naming it with sufficient precision.<1>p. 587</1>
They help locate where the problem happens. They say less about how it is produced in legally relevant terms.<1>p. 588</1>

Semiotic vulnerability takes as its problem the unequal administration of meaning, and the gain is dogmatic, because the duty to inform is measured by decisional usefulness, advertising is controlled by ambiguity and relevant omission, transparency comes closer to verifiability and architecture may be qualified, where applicable, as the form of the abuse.
The category targets a mechanism, not a setting.<1>p. 588</1>
The legally relevant problem becomes the unequal administration of meaning, that is, the way the platform organizes the conditions of intelligibility of the consumer experience itself.<1>p. 588</1>

The duty to inform can be reconstructed as a requirement of adequacy and decisional usefulness, and not as a mere volume of data. Advertising becomes controllable by criteria of ambiguity, relevant omission, identification and truthfulness. Transparency stops being a shop-window word and comes closer to a requirement of institutional verifiability. And the architecture of supply may be qualified, where applicable, not only as the context of the abuse, but as its own structured form of production. The gain is not aesthetic. It is dogmatic.<1>p. 590</1>
How should one read the literature that speaks of digital vulnerability?

The review has a controlled scope, with no claim to exhaustiveness, and reads each work on four points, whether there was a definition or only an invocation, which concrete asymmetry was described, whether there was a reconstructible evidentiary standard and which legal consequence was triggered. The first result is one of recognition. Palmeira links digital vulnerability to the monetization of data, attention, behavioral advertising and dark patterns, and Furtado and Pinto, to lengthy terms of use, data assignment and the appearance of gratuity, which shows that the problem was already recognized.
The scope does not aim at exhaustiveness. It aims at minimal verifiability.<1>p. 591</1>

In each work, it was tested whether “digital vulnerability” named only the setting in which the problem arises or whether it effectively identified the legally relevant mechanism of the asymmetry. From there, four points were observed: whether there was a definition or only an invocation; which concrete asymmetry was described; whether the text indicated any minimally reconstructible evidentiary standard; and which normative structure or legal consequence was triggered.<1>p. 592</1>

The first result of the survey is that recent literature correctly perceived the intensification of the consumer's fragility in platform environments. This appears clearly in more robust formulations, which link so-called digital vulnerability to the monetization of data, the centrality of attention, behavioral advertising, dark patterns and decision-making opacity distributed along the consumer journey <1>Palmeira</1><2>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 230; p. 15; p. 143-144)</2><3>p. 592-593</3>

It also appears in works that describe the consumer's vulnerabilization based on lengthy terms of use, data assignment, the appearance of gratuity, opaque language and decision acceleration on digital platforms <1>Pinto</1><2>(Furtado; Pinto, 2024, p. 13; p. 12; p. 21)</2><3>p. 593</3>
The problem, therefore, is not an invention of the thesis. The field already sees that something important has changed.<1>p. 593</1>

These works draw legal effect from the category. Palmeira draws from it the universalization of hyposufficiency and of the reversal of the burden of proof, and Furtado and Pinto argue for the abusiveness of unrestricted authorization of data processing as consideration in zero-price models. The limit pointed out is that the consequence tends to be drawn wholesale, from the global perception of a hostile environment, and not from a specific mechanism, when what is appropriate is the rational redistribution of the burden.

The critical usefulness of the expression “consumer's digital vulnerability” does not disappear because it shows low maximal refinement as an explanatory category. On the contrary, its recent circulation shows a real effort to draw concrete protective consequences in the consumer field, especially when arguing for the abusiveness of unrestricted authorization for data processing as consideration imposed in zero-price models, even if formally provided for in terms of use <1>Pinto</1><2>(Furtado; Pinto, 2024, p. 23)</2>.<3>p. 594</3>

The literature reviewed is relevant and, in several cases, normatively ambitious. But the label “digital vulnerability” or its close equivalents works, most of the time, better as a summary of the setting than as an isolator of the legally central mechanism. Sometimes it produces a concrete protective consequence, such as the defense of a stronger reversal of the burden of proof or expanded contractual control. Even so, this consequence tends to be drawn wholesale, from the global perception of a hostile environment, and not from the more precise stabilization of the specific mechanism of asymmetry.<1>p. 600</1>

Leonardo Machado Acosta proposes cybervulnerability, which records the aggravation, in cyberspace, of already known vulnerabilities. The proposal shows real merit and a serious effort to juridify the problem through the CDC and the Constitution, although it remains tied to cyberspace as its axis.

The notion of “cybervulnerability” registers, quite perceptively, that cyberspace aggravates vulnerabilities already known and widens the power gap between consumer and supplier, including through factors such as insufficient literacy, informational asymmetry, data collection and manipulation of the will <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86; p. 93; p. 97; p. 120; p. 83-84)</2><3>p. 595</3>

There is real merit in this. But the category itself remains closely attached to the technological setting as its organizing principle, which makes it less sharp for isolating the specific legal mechanism of vulnerabilization it seeks to explain. The author even seeks juridicization through the CDC and the Constitution, which shows a serious effort at normativity, but the formulation still coexists with a strong dependence on “cyberspace” as its structural axis <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93; p. 113; p. 119)</2>.<3>p. 595</3>

Azevedo and Torres address situational digital hypervulnerability in games, identify real mechanisms such as captivity, design adapted to behavior and irregular rewards, and end up treating the family unit as equivalent to the child under Article 29 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>. The limit is its dependence on the public affected and on the context in which it applies.

The literature identifies, with relevant precision, real mechanisms that aggravate vulnerability on platforms, such as continuous data collection, dynamic architecture, adaptation of design to user behavior, captivity, situational monopoly, irregular rewards and immersion strategies <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 8; p. 23; p. 15-16; p. 11; p. 21)</2>.<3>p. 596</3>

In this dimension, Azevedo and Torres's formulation does not remain entirely on the sociological plane, since the authors seek to link it to specific protective responses within the consumer and constitutional system. This appears when they argue for the “hypervulnerability of the family unit” by treating it as equivalent to the child under art. 29 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, approaching the family as a collectivity exposed to commercial practices that, although they initially reach minors, radiate effects across the whole family unit and weaken the exercise of parental authority <3>Torres</3><4>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 22)</4>.<5>p. 597</5>

There is even some normative density, with protective consequences drawn for cases involving children, family and market practices in digital games <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 22-23)</2><3>p. 596-597</3>
Even so, the category remains heavily dependent on the public affected and on the specific context in which it applies.<1>p. 597</1>
Maia and Simões use the vocabulary to name real barriers to access to justice and real forms of technical exclusion, a serious and current usage, but a polysemous one.

The analysis of the vocabulary of “electronic” or “technological vulnerability” reinforces the same diagnosis. Such expressions are useful for naming real barriers created by the compulsory digitalization of services, channels and procedures, especially in access to justice and in the technical exclusion of certain groups <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 3; p. 2)</2><3>p. 597</3>

There is also an important contrast with the field of access to justice. There, the expression “digital vulnerability” circulates to designate phenomena of technical exclusion, lack of access, skills deficits and barriers to inclusion in digitalized environments, especially for more socially exposed groups <1>Simões</1><2>(Simões, 2024, p. 79; p. 83; p. 86)</2><3>p. 598</3>
This confirms that the vocabulary is serious, current and relevant. But it also confirms its polysemy.<1>p. 598</1>

The yardstick comes from Wada, for whom what matters is whether there is functional opacity capable of compromising understanding and choice, including when the information exists and the form of presentation strips it of usefulness. Hence the refinement criterion with four cumulative requirements, identifying a mechanism and not only a context, converting it into a duty, an unlawful act or a criterion of control, offering a minimally reconstructible evidentiary standard and pointing to a typical consequence compatible with the system.

The contrast with the work of Ricardo Morishita Wada helps clarify this point. The legally relevant problem does not lie in the relationship taking place in a sophisticated technological universe, but in whether there is functional opacity capable of compromising the consumer's understanding, choice and practical self-determination. Informational failure does not stem only from the absence of data; it may also arise when the information exists, but the way it is presented neutralizes its practical usefulness, reduces transparency, hinders comparison or compromises understanding <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 168; p. 193-194; p. 213-214)</2>.<3>p. 599</3>

To operate dogmatically within the CDC, any category of vulnerability must satisfy at least four cumulative requirements: identify a mechanism, and not only a context; convert this mechanism into a duty, an unlawful act or a criterion of control; offer a minimally reconstructible evidentiary standard; and point to a typical consequence compatible with the structure of the protective system. When these elements do not appear, the category may remain useful as a diagnosis of the environment, but remains weak as a decision concept.<1>p. 600</1>
How does meaning vitiate consent?

The CDC already contains the core of the problem. Article 31 of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1> requires the offer to ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information in Portuguese, and Article 46 of the CDC<3><4>5</4></3> provides that contracts do not bind the consumer without an opportunity for prior knowledge or when drafted so as to hinder understanding of their meaning and scope. That is why the decisive point is not proving that the text was there, but assessing whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms.

“Art. 31. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information, in the Portuguese language, about their characteristics, qualities, quantity, composition, price, warranty, expiry dates and origin, among other data, as well as about the risks they present to the health and safety of consumers.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 601</3>

“Art. 46. Contracts that regulate consumer relations shall not bind consumers if they are not given the opportunity to become aware of their content beforehand, or if the respective instruments are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 601</3>

Language is not a neutral vehicle. Warat observes that the coherent organization of a discourse can silence problems, and on platforms contractual language acts together with interface, sign-up flow and placement of links, which steer the user to accept before understanding. This is where meaning-vitiated consent arises, which is not a one-off factual error, such as confusing a price, but an inability structurally produced, by the communicational conditions of supply, to decode, compare and anticipate relevant consequences.
The consumer may be formally informed and, even so, materially cut off from the meaning of what they accept.<1>p. 604</1>

The “coherent organization of a discourse” can “silence problems” and, through these silences, fulfill “political functions in society”, while at the same time it “explicitly forces subjects to say or repress certain things” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 50)</2>.<3>p. 602</3>

Legal and institutional language is not neutral. It operates as a technique for producing and stabilizing meaning, immersed in political and strategic factors, which dispels the image of contracts or interfaces as mere transparent containers of information.<1>p. 602</1>

On platforms, this is especially important, because contractual language does not come alone. It acts together with interface, sign-up flow, selective highlighting of information, placement of links and visual framings that steer the consumer to accept before understanding.<1>p. 602-603</1>

It is at this point that one can speak of meaning-vitiated consent. It is not a one-off factual error, such as confusing a price or an isolated deadline.
