It is an inability structurally produced, by the communicational conditions of supply, to decode, compare and anticipate relevant consequences.<1>p. 603-604</1>

The duty to inform becomes material. The supplier does not fulfill it merely by making the content accessible by click or scroll, and what matters is whether the average consumer could understand what the clauses meant and what consequences followed from adhering. Obscurity, in this picture, is evidence of structural disloyalty in the organization of consent. Claudia Lima Marques reads predisposed clauses through Article 47 of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1> and the general clause of Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<3><4>7</4></3>, so as to respect the trust of those who accepted them, and links the sanction of Article 46 of the CDC<5><6>5</6></5> to the presumption of bad faith of the supplier who drafted the contract.

The supplier does not fulfill this duty merely because it made the content technically accessible by click, scroll or download. What matters is whether the average consumer could read and understand what those clauses meant, which rights and obligations were being assumed and which practical consequences followed from adhering.<1>p. 604</1>

The principle of transparency, in this picture, is not a peripheral formality. It affects the very essence of the transaction, because information is part of the content of the contract and, if it fails, it compromises the legal quality of the performance. This explains why contractual obscurity, in consumption, is not an innocent stylistic flaw. It is evidence of structural disloyalty in the organization of consent.<1>p. 604</1>

With pre-drafted clauses, the consumer takes no part in formulating the text and frequently enters the relationship trusting that the wording respects a minimum of loyalty and intelligibility. That is why the new function of contract law restores to a central position the principle of interpretation in accordance with good faith, so that art. 47 of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1>, together with the general clause of art. 51, IV, allows predisposed clauses to be interpreted "in a way that respects the trust and the legitimate interests of the consumers who accepted these pre-drafted clauses" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 94-95)</4>.<5>p. 604-605</5>

The dogmatic consequence is twofold. First, the duty to inform must be read as a duty of intelligibility, adequacy and verifiability, and not as the mere delivery of documentary volume. Second, consumer protection in platform environments requires standards capable of reducing at the same time the asymmetry of meaning and the asymmetry of proof.<1>p. 605</1>
How does vulnerability appear in excess information and in advertising?

The regime of information and advertising is the subject of its own chapter, and here the two figures matter as manifestations of vulnerability. Performative transparency is information that exists, but in excess, dispersion and faulty ranking of the essential, so that the supplier appears to fulfill the duty through abundance. Layers of documents, cross-references, inverted visual emphasis and cascading notices may produce the same effect as omission, and Article 54, paragraphs 3 and 4, of the CDC, which requires clear terms and highlighting for limiting clauses, prevents the essential from being hidden. The defense that everything was in the terms turns the duty to inform into a documentary treasure hunt, which the CDC does not allow.
Adequate information is not the information that exists in some remote corner of the system.<1>p. 621</1>

Performative transparency does not consist in the absence of information, but in excess, dispersion and faulty ranking of the essential content. The supplier appears to fulfill the legal duty through abundance, but the communicational design reduces the practical usefulness of what it presents.<1>p. 620</1>

“§ 3 Written adhesion contracts shall be drafted in clear terms and with conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding by the consumer. § 4 Clauses that imply a limitation of the consumer's rights shall be drafted with emphasis, allowing their immediate and easy understanding.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 621</3>

The typical defense holds that the consumer could have read everything calmly, needing only to click more, open more links, follow more cross-references or consult FAQs and supplementary policies. The problem with this defense is that it turns the duty to inform into an obligation of documentary treasure hunting on the consumer's part. The CDC does not allow this.<1>p. 621-622</1>

For immaterial objects, advertising announces a governed future experience and may produce error through the semiotic construction of a trust incompatible with the regime of enjoyment. Adalberto Pasqualotto notes that deceptiveness does not depend on literal falsehood and may arise from a partly true message, through omission, ambiguity or the way it is presented. Article 38 of the CDC<1><2>8</2></1> places on whoever sponsors the communication the burden of proving its truthfulness and correctness, and it follows that, if the platform announces a certain equivalence or rarity, it is up to the platform to prove with documents that the narrative is correct.
Fair advertising is not merely advertising “without lies”.<1>p. 625</1>

For IOCs, advertising does not announce only an object. It announces a governed future experience. And, for that very reason, it may produce error not only through express falsehood, but through the semiotic construction of a trust incompatible with the reality of the regime of enjoyment.<1>p. 624</1>

Advertising deceptiveness, in the CDC, does not depend on literal falsehood or on a frontally demonstrable lie. Unlawfulness may arise whenever the message, even if partly true, is apt to lead the consumer into error, including through omission, ambiguity, relevant incompleteness or the very form of presentation of the content <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 167)</2>.<3>p. 626</3>
“Art. 38. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 627</3>

If the platform announces a certain equivalence, a certain benefit, a certain utility, a certain standard of stability or a certain implicit value of rarity, it is for the platform to demonstrate in documents the correctness of this narrative against what is ordinarily delivered and administered in the ecosystem.<1>p. 627</1>

The regulation of advertising to children enters as a limit case, without equating adults with children, because it shows that the CDC itself recognizes as legally relevant the exploitation of a structural deficiency of judgment. Transposed in a controlled way, the reasoning holds that private governance of meaning can also produce real asymmetries of decoding, comparison and proof, and that, when systematically exploited, they open room for reinforced control, which strengthens the reading of semiotic vulnerability as a legal fact.

The point is not to equate adults with children, nor to open a new thematic front. The point is to show that the CDC itself already recognizes that abusiveness may stem from taking advantage of a structural deficiency of judgment exploited by persuasive communication.<1>p. 628</1>

Transposing this reasoning in a controlled way to IOCs, without infantilizing the adult consumer, the argument is that there are also situations in which architecture, curation and private governance of meaning produce real asymmetries of decoding, comparison and proof. When these asymmetries are systematically exploited by advertising and by the platform's communicational environment, room opens for reinforced control of deceptiveness and abusiveness.<1>p. 628</1>
This reinforces, from within the system itself, the legitimacy of treating semiotic vulnerability as a legal fact and not as a sociological metaphor.<1>p. 628</1>
What must be shown to assert semiotic vulnerability in a case?

Once the category is converted into a parameter, three readings are ruled out, that of a generic attribute of the digital, that of economic hyposufficiency and that of lesser individual aptitude, because all of them shift the problem to the person of the user and hide the structure of power. The term designates a mechanism inscribed in the architecture of supply, by which the supplier administers the modes of presentation of the object, the visibility of relevant information, the routes of understanding and the possibilities of reaction. The asymmetry of meaning tends to come with an asymmetry of proof, because whoever controls the intelligibility of the object frequently controls the records through which it can be reconstructed, and there is a double concentration here, that of shaping the reading of enjoyment and that of narrating retrospectively what happened.
It is not a matter of asking whether the user was sufficiently attentive, distrustful or technically informed.<1>p. 720</1>

The vulnerability relevant to the application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption cannot be understood as a generic attribute of the digital, nor be reduced to economic hyposufficiency or to the consumer's lesser individual aptitude to understand technically complex environments. This reading is insufficient because it shifts the problem to the person of the user and obscures the structure of power that shapes the relationship.<1>p. 719</1>

The term does not designate the consumer's naivety, credulity or cultural deficiency. It designates a mechanism of power inscribed in the architecture of supply, through which the supplier administers the modes of presentation of the object, the criteria of visibility of relevant information, the routes of understanding of the experience, the perceived equivalences and the practical possibilities of resistance or reaction.<1>p. 719-720</1>

The result is a double concentration of power. On one side, it concentrates the capacity to shape the ordinary reading of enjoyment. On the other, it concentrates the capacity to narrate retrospectively, in institutionally acceptable terms, what happened in the relationship.<1>p. 720</1>

In concrete terms, two things are shown. The first is the arrangement, because it is not enough that the case involves an interface, an algorithm or an online environment, and signs, paths and records must be organized asymmetrically by whoever can also alter, sanction or modulate the relationship. The second is the interference, because the category, relational, structural and functional, only takes on dogmatic relevance when it interferes with the formation of expectation, the reading of utility, the assessment of risk or the consumer's possibility of institutional reaction.

It is not enough that the case involves an interface, an algorithm or an online environment. The governance of meaning must act structurally on the understanding, comparability, predictability or contestation of enjoyment. What is controlled, therefore, is not the mere existence of technological mediation, but the configuration of an arrangement in which signs, paths and records are asymmetrically organized by whoever also holds the power to alter, sanction or modulate the relationship.<1>p. 721</1>

Semiotic vulnerability is relational, structural and functional. Relational, because it arises from the position occupied by the parties in the production and administration of meaning. Structural, because it stems from the design of the environment and not only from isolated episodes. Functional, because it only takes on dogmatic relevance when it interferes with the formation of expectation, the reading of utility, the assessment of risk or the consumer's possibility of institutional reaction.<1>p. 721</1>

What has to be shown is concrete. Proof of informational adequacy depends on minimal documentation of the purchase flow, the confirmation screens, the change notices, the way equivalences are presented and the visual placement of the limitations, and the platform must be in a position to show how, when and with what emphasis it informed. Since these records lie with the supplier, the allocation of the burden cannot remain blind to the asymmetry, and requests for preservation and disclosure are the subject of the chapter on proof.
When proof of this informational regime is concentrated in the supplier, the distribution of the burden cannot remain blind to this asymmetry.<1>p. 623</1>
Isn't this psychologizing the consumer?

The first objection is psychologizing. But semiotic vulnerability does not describe lesser individual discernment or subjective susceptibility. It describes the objective way in which the environment organizes language, visibility, comparison and proof, and it is neither a moral judgment about whoever did not read nor an explanation by impulse or addiction. The neighboring objection, of moralism against the symbolic or against advertising, has a similar answer, because the problem is not desiring the object or attributing symbolic value to it, but the expectation organized toward an image that the regime of supply does not sustain.

Semiotic vulnerability does not describe the user's lesser individual discernment, psychological naivety or subjective susceptibility. The problem lies in the objective way in which the environment organizes language, visibility, comparison and proof.<1>p. 580</1>

This vulnerability is also not to be confused with a moral judgment of the consumer who “did not read” or “did not understand”, because the problem is not a lack of attention before a text, but an asymmetry over the bases that make the promise operative and over the possibility of reconstructing them with proof. Nor is it reduced to a psychologizing of behavior, as if everything were explained by impulse, desire or “addiction”, since permanence is produced by an architecture of comparison and by governance of time, and not by mere spontaneous affect.<1>p. 321</1>

The problem is not desiring, fantasizing or attributing symbolic value to the object. The problem is when the marketing production of expectation is organized so as to steer the consumer's understanding toward an image of the object that the regime of supply itself does not sustain, or sustains only under hidden reservations, opaque equivalences and silent mutability.<1>p. 629</1>

Another foreseeable objection is that every consumer is already vulnerable and the concept adds nothing. The premise is true, since vulnerability is the starting point of the system and the treatise by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa speaks of a presumption of vulnerability in favor of the natural person who is the final recipient. What the category adds is the mechanism, because it locates the asymmetry in the production and governance of meaning, and operable consequences follow from this, information measured by its usefulness for decisions, advertising that can be controlled for ambiguity and relevant omission, and proof that requires trails to be preserved.

Vulnerability is the starting point of the system and militates in favor of the final recipient precisely because the market is organized by asymmetries that the consumer does not control <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 168; p. 118; p. 166])</2>.<3>p. 553</3>

The Manual recovers Antonio Herman Benjamin's formulation according to which vulnerability is the “fundamental piece” and the “starting point” of all application of consumer law, especially in contractual matters, which is why, in light of arts. 2 and 4, I, a true presumption of vulnerability militates in favor of natural persons who are final recipients of products and services <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 168])</2>.<3>p. 553</3>

The adoption of “semiotic vulnerability” responds to this problem. It does not replace “digital vulnerability” out of mere vocabulary whim. It replaces a predominantly environmental category with another aimed at describing the mechanism.<1>p. 600</1>

The relevant asymmetry comes to be located in the production and governance of meaning, that is, in the way the platform administers expectation, perception of value, perception of risk, comparability, intelligibility of the offer and conditions of contestation. The result is greater operability. Information is no longer thought of as volume and comes to be thought of as decisional usefulness and verifiability. Advertising is no longer a mere promotional background and becomes controllable by ambiguity and relevant omission.<1>p. 600-601</1>

The objection that the supplier disclosed the risk in the terms of use runs into the observation that formal clarifications describe the risk in generic terms and do not give the consumer back equivalent means to understand, verify and contest the decisions that reconfigure their position. The objection of trivialization, that everything digital would become vulnerability, meets the delimiting function of the parameter, and the charge of terminological fussiness is answered by the fact that the gain is operational, and not a dispute over labels.

Even when there are formal clarifications about rules of use or about abstract possibilities of alteration, the decisive asymmetry remains when the environment keeps for itself the administration of the codes of valuation, the regimes of visibility and the internal criteria that qualify conduct and distribute consequences. Informing, in this picture, describes the risk in generic terms, but does not give the consumer back equivalent means to understand, verify and contest the decisions that reconfigure their position.<1>p. 406-407</1>
The parameter also has a delimiting function. It prevents every difficulty experienced in a digital environment from being automatically converted into legally qualified vulnerability.<1>p. 721</1>

And abusiveness may, when necessary, be reconstructed at the level of the very architecture of supply. It is this operational gain, and not a dispute over labels, that justifies the terminological substitution adopted here.<1>p. 601</1>
Does every change become a loss?

The normality of change is a premise of the category, and not an objection to it. The category does not turn every change of catalog or visibility into a loss, and the question it raises concerns the conditions under which a change can be treated as compatible with the promise and with the preservation of the relevant value. For the same reason, a nerf is not presumed unlawful. It is examined as a downgrade whose compatibility with the promise is hard to assess when the very criterion of what counts as delivery remains under unilateral administration.

In reconfigurable markets, altering the catalog, reordering visibility, redesigning cycles and recalibrating signals make up the regular mode of governance, but this normality cannot work as a license to preserve continuity of appearance while the core of the position of enjoyment is shifted from within.<1>p. 330</1>

The question that matters is not whether the game can be adjusted, but under what conditions the platform can treat as “compatible with the promise” a substantive downgrade of delivery, when the very criterion of what counts as delivery remains under unilateral administration and with traces whose form and sufficiency are also defined by the same authority.<1>p. 329</1>

The symbolic enters the comparison only to the extent that it was an operative condition of the position bought, and no symbolic value is turned into an indeterminate legal obligation. The trace required is that of whatever is material to the position of enjoyment acquired, and not a generic trade secret. Nor does the category replace the criteria of control or prove abuse by itself, because what it does is identify the asymmetry and make manageable institutional verifiability, adequacy read in terms of functional integrity and a more realistic allocation of the burden.

Since, in the IOC, part of the value is materially produced by recognition and commensurability in the ecosystem, the “functional” also covers this component only to the extent that it was an operative condition of the position bought, that is, that without which the good stops working as a recognizable difference in the relevant terms of the acquisition. This does not authorize turning any symbolic value into an indeterminate legal obligation; on the contrary, it requires isolating what was relevant to that specific position and comparing whether the restoration preserved this core or merely kept signs of continuity while shifting, from within, what mattered.<1>p. 327</1>

What must leave a trace is not a generic “trade secret”, but whatever is material to the position of enjoyment acquired, such as criteria of classification and reading of the item, parameters that organize visibility and comparison, rules and metrics that sustain recognition and belonging, and temporal decisions that shape access, cadence and relevance.<1>p. 326</1>

Semiotic vulnerability neither replaces the standards formulated nor merges with them. It identifies the relevant structural asymmetry in IOCs and allows the problem to be led back to classic CDC categories without reducing the controversy to a “mere environmental problem” external to the object. From it, the following steps of the argument become manageable, in particular the requirement of institutional verifiability, the reconstruction of adequacy in terms of functional integrity and a more realistic distribution of the burden of proof in the face of opaque and governed mutations of enjoyment.<1>p. 584</1>

The distinction between the structural and strategic faces serves to identify when the structure of the ecosystem is mobilized for exploitative purposes without depending on an express contractual command, a step that belongs to the chapter on abusive teleology. The stronger expressions also have a declared limit, because identity captivity does not designate physical imprisonment, social death is a functional description, Han's usefulness is descriptive and the transposition of advertising to children does not infantilize the adult.

The distinction between these faces makes it possible to recognize that semiotic vulnerability is not limited to an inevitable setting of technical mediation, but also provides language to identify when the structure of the ecosystem is mobilized in a way oriented to exploitative purposes, without this identification depending on express contractual commands or on ostensibly abusive textual promises.<1>p. 403-404</1>

The usefulness is descriptive. The categories proposed by Han make it possible to name how information technologies, metrics and regimes of visibility convert adherence, self-adjustment and continuous comparison into stable conformity, above all in environments in which recognition and permanence become conditions of value.<1>p. 352</1>

Architecture and governance are part of supply

Architecture and governance are part of supply itself and are not a neutral setting. It is through architecture that the platform defines paths, frictions, salience, reversibility and costs of understanding, and it is through governance that it administers permanence, sanction, updating, priority, visibility and contestation. Making this structure invisible reduces the debate to the final acts of an environment that has already predetermined much of the disputed experience.
It is through governance that the supplier administers permanence, sanction, updating, priority, visibility and mechanisms of contestation.<1>p. 749</1>
Alterations are judged by auditability and equivalence

Significant alterations, rule changes and reconfigurations with material impact are not judged by the generic discourse of updating, innovation or technical convenience. They are examined through open auditability and functional value equivalence. The question is whether the alteration was made intelligible and whether it preserved the function that justified the acquisition, and not only whether the platform was allowed to make it.
They must be examined in light of open auditability and functional value equivalence.<1>p. 749</1>
The relevant question is not only whether the platform could make the change.<1>p. 749</1>
Sanctions require reasons and real contestation

Private sanctions may affect access, permanence, visibility, reputation, relational insertion and continuity of enjoyment. That is why they require verifiable reasons, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of contestation. The procedure must be reconstructible, and contestation cannot be an empty ritual. The examination also reaches the procedural conditions the supplier designed for adhesion, enjoyment, proof and resistance.
They require verifiable reasons, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of contestation.<1>p. 749</1>
The case is read along its trajectory

The controversy is reconstructed from the environment in which it arose, and not only from the moment it became visible. Judges and protection bodies consider how the platform organized, from the start, adhesion, understanding, circulation of information, access to records and contestation. The case is seen along its trajectory, and not only in its outcome.

This means that judges and protection bodies need to consider how the platform organized, from the start, the conditions of adhesion, understanding, circulation of information, access to records and possibility of contestation.<1>p. 750</1>
Opacity is not a procedural privilege

Structural opacity should not be treated as an inevitable and neutral feature of digital complexity. It is a factor that intensifies vulnerability and evidentiary asymmetry. It justifies orders to preserve and disclose minimal records, delimitation of expert examinations and dynamic redistribution of the burden whenever the relevant evidence arises and remains under the supplier's technical control.
It must be recognized as a factor that intensifies vulnerability and evidentiary asymmetry.<1>p. 750</1>

This fact justifies orders to preserve and disclose minimal records, delimitation of expert examinations and dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof whenever the relevant evidence arises and remains under the supplier's technical control.<1>p. 750</1>
Neither fragment the case nor turn it into a manifesto

Control avoids both fragmentation into individual lawsuits unable to reach the source of the injury and turning each case into a manifesto against technology. It must distinguish individual inadequacy, correctable without further expansion, from a regime defect, repeatable and embedded in ordinary operation. This distinction calibrates the response.
Neither atomization nor grandiloquence.<1>p. 750</1>

Control must be specific enough to respond to the concrete conflict and attentive enough to the structure to recognize when this conflict is a localized manifestation of a repeated pattern.<1>p. 750</1>
Restore before compensating

In architectural injury, the response favors functional restoration and procedural correction. Whenever possible, restoration of access, reversal or review of sanctions, restoration of functionality, preservation of history, equivalent substitution and adjustment of governance procedures are appropriate.
A repeated pattern calls for regime correction

When the pattern of injury is repeated, replicable and embedded in the structure, protection is not limited to the single case. The way opens for injunctive relief and regime correction, with procedural duties, architecture adjustments, reinforced auditability, review of sanction flows and intelligible channels of contestation.
When the pattern of injury proves repeated, replicable and embedded in the structure of the environment, protection should not be limited to the single case.<1>p. 751</1>
This includes procedural duties, architecture adjustments, reinforced auditability requirements, review of sanction flows, imposition of intelligible channels of contestation<1>p. 751</1>
The judge need not become an engineer

Control does not require the judge to become the system's engineer. It requires bringing the environment back under verifiable filters of legitimacy. Open auditability, functional equivalence, verifiable reasons, procedural coherence, intelligibility of contestation, preservation of records and reconciliation between exclusivity and protection are enough to make the conflict decidable.
The complexity of the digital does not eliminate Law. It only requires Law to choose more rigorously what it needs to understand in order to control.<1>p. 751</1>
Supply, proof and remedy are one problem

Supply, proof and remedy cannot be rigidly separated. The offer shapes the perception of loss, governance conditions proof, and the distribution of access and opacity affects the adequacy of the remedy. Separating these planes produces decisions that are organized in form and blind in substance.
Finally, a tenth guideline requires that institutional examination preserve unity between supply, proof and remedy.<1>p. 751</1>
